analysis.one_liner: Requires the biggest banks to stop financing new fossil fuel projects and cut financed emissions to zero by 2050.
analysis.headline: The Fossil Free Finance Act was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in September 2021 and never advanced; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large banks — those with $50 billion or more in assets — to submit plans to the Federal Reserve for cutting the emissions their lending and investments finance: a 50% cut by 2030 and zero by 2050, with no carbon offsets counted. It would have ordered banks to stop financing new or expanded fossil fuel projects by 2023, thermal coal by 2025, and all fossil fuels by 2030, with penalties including forced divestment and possible loss of deposit insurance. The House committee it was sent to never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities near new fossil fuel infrastructure and everyone exposed to climate change, since the bill would have cut the flow of Wall Street money into new oil, gas, and coal projects. Workers in fossil fuel industries were addressed directly: banks would have had to finance severance and retraining for those displaced, and the Federal Reserve would have had to study the transition's economic impact and recommend support.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Climate-exposed communities; displaced fossil fuel workers

how_it_helps.text: Required the largest banks to submit Federal Reserve-approved plans to cut their financed emissions 50% by 2030 and reach zero by 2050, with no carbon offsets allowed to count.
Required banks to stop financing new or expanded fossil fuel projects (pipelines, wells, terminals, refineries) by 2023, end thermal coal financing by 2025, and end all fossil fuel financing by 2030.

Directed banks to prioritize pulling funding from polluters that disproportionately harm low-income and minority communities, and to fund severance and retraining for workers displaced by the transition.
Backed the requirements with real enforcement: the Fed could impose penalties, force divestiture, and the FDIC could terminate deposit insurance for noncompliant banks.

analysis.who_pays: Large banks, which would face new planning, disclosure, and divestment requirements and penalties up to losing FDIC deposit insurance, and fossil fuel companies and their workers, who would lose access to bank financing for new projects. Some regions dependent on fossil fuel activity could see credit tighten, though the bill aimed to soften that with worker transition funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks and fossil fuel producers

drawbacks.text: Banking regulators, not climate agencies, would enforce energy policy: the Federal Reserve could force asset divestitures and the FDIC could terminate deposit insurance for noncompliant banks, an unusual use of financial-safety tools to steer lending decisions.

Cutting off financing for new fossil fuel projects, including pipelines and terminals, could raise costs or create supply bottlenecks in regions and industries that depend on those fuels during the transition.

The bill reached only a first-stage introduction with no committee action, so its practical workability — how 'science-based targets' would be measured for individual banks, for example — was never tested in hearings or a floor debate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have forced large banks to stop financing new fossil fuel expansion, which climate science and the bill's own findings treat as necessary to meet the 1.5°C target, while requiring worker retraining and protection for overburdened communities. The costs are real: lenders and fossil fuel companies would lose access to capital for some projects, and some communities that depend on fossil energy would face disruption the bill tries to but cannot fully cushion. The core drawback is political and design: banking regulators would be enforcing energy policy, an unusual mandate, and opponents argued it could restrict credit. No up-or-down vote ever tested these tradeoffs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee when introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Mondaire Jones introduced the Fossil Free Finance Act on September 14, 2021, with 14 original cosponsors including Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Pressley, Tlaib, and Jayapal.
It gathered 20 cosponsors, all Democrats, and was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced.

The complete action history contains only the introduction and the committee referral — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and the fossil fuel industry, which continue financing new oil, gas, and coal projects without the restrictions the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big banks and fossil fuel companies

for.name: 20 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all Democrats including Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Pressley, Tlaib, and Jayapal.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Maxine Waters)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote after the referral.

against.name: Large banks and financial industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory climate-financing mandates as an intrusion into lending decisions.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Democratic-led Financial Services Committee never scheduled action on the bill.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies (over $50 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed binding emission-reduction plans, new fossil fuel financing bans, and divestiture and insurance-termination penalties on roughly the largest US banks, forcing them to restructure lending and underwriting. It never became law, so their ability to finance fossil fuel expansion was never restricted.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel companies (oil, gas, and coal producers and pipeline operators)
industries.note: The bill's central mechanism was cutting off bank financing for new and expanded fossil fuel projects, thermal coal by 2025, and all fossil fuel financing by 2030. It died in committee, so fossil fuel companies kept full access to Wall Street capital.
